CardNeuro

Live · iOS Fintech · Rewards

The right credit card for every checkout, decided before you reach the till.

Visit cardneuro.com →

Why we’re building this

  • It started with my own wallet.
  • I held four credit cards and, standing at a checkout, I couldn’t remember which one earned the most — so I paid with whichever was handy, even though I knew some paid far higher rates on dining and groceries.
  • Checkout is the wrong place to make that decision.
  • CardNeuro makes it before you arrive.

The problem with current apps

  • Rewards sites list rates in static tables that ignore merchant-specific offers, quarterly rotations, caps and channel rules — and they answer a research question, not a checkout question.
  • Bank apps each show only their own card.
  • Nobody combines all your cards, all your transactions, and the place you’re standing in into one answer in the two seconds it’s needed.

What it solves

  • Decides at the moment of payment: GPS detects the merchant and recommends the highest-earning card from your actual wallet, opening Apple Wallet instantly.
  • Matches the way rewards really work: suggestions match on merchant + category + channel, in order — a merchant-gated rate first, then the general category rate, then the all-other rate — and show the reason (“2× on United flights”).
  • Proves its value: bank connections via Mastercard Finicity bring every card’s transactions into one place, tracking rewards earned vs. missed and powering spending analytics.
  • Grounds recommendations in verified data: a hand-verified database of 678 cards and 1,769 reward rows, refreshed quarterly, with non-cash-back units never mislabelled as “% cash back.”

Monetization strategy

  • Free for users — distribution first, with a goal of 1,000 users in the first three months.
  • Revenue comes from card-issuer affiliate partnerships when a recommendation leads to an application, which only works if recommendations stay provably in the user’s interest: the highest-earning card wins, every time, whether it pays us or not.

Marketing strategy

  • LinkedIn is the primary channel: daily posts on the personal profile with the App Store link in the first comment, plus a company-page launch sequence.
  • A 36-article SEO plan (per-merchant “best card” guides, rotating-category pages, card-vs-card comparisons) compounds search traffic, and the #MyMoneyStory campaign carries the story to TikTok and Instagram Reels for a Gen Z, credit-building audience.

InvoiceNest

Built · Pre-launch Freelancer Suite · Productivity

Invoice, quote and track time — offline, with no account and no subscription.

App Store link — added at launch

Why we’re building this

  • Freelancers don’t have an invoicing problem — they have a getting-paid problem.
  • Invoices get written late, in whatever tool is open, and chased later still.
  • InvoiceNest is built around the two moments that decide cash flow: creating the invoice in under a minute, and turning tracked time into that invoice without re-typing anything.

The problem with current apps

  • Mainstream invoicing tools have become subscription accounting suites: monthly fees, mandatory cloud accounts, onboarding wizards, and feature depth a solo freelancer never touches.
  • The free tiers watermark or cap invoices.
  • A one-person business ends up renting basic paperwork — and its client list sits on someone else’s server.

What it solves

  • Fast, list-first invoicing: five tabs (Home, Invoices, Quotes, Clients, Settings), generous white space, and invoice creation measured in seconds.
  • Time becomes money automatically: a timer that survives app restarts converts tracked time straight into invoice lines.
  • Clients saved once: a dedicated Clients tab — save a contact once, pick it in any invoice or quote.
  • Professional chasing: a proper reminder sheet with a preview, sent by email or text, and quote → invoice conversion in one tap.
  • Yours, offline: everything stored on-device in SQLite; PDF generation and sharing built in; no account, works on a plane.

Monetization strategy

  • The app is free — reach is the asset.
  • Revenue comes from two directions that don’t tax the core job: affiliate referrals freelancers genuinely need (business banking, tax, insurance), and paid add-ons for power users — premium templates and logo branding, cloud backup/sync, and QuickBooks/Xero export.
  • No ads, no upfront charge.

Marketing strategy

  • A free invoice-generator web tool is the SEO funnel: it ranks for the exact query a freelancer types the day they need their first invoice, and the app is the upgrade.
  • Community distribution follows a strict 9:1 helpful-to-promotional rule on Reddit, with a Product Hunt launch, short-form video demos, Facebook freelancer groups, and LinkedIn.
  • Launch order: US first, then Canada, Australia and Europe.

Daily Life Suite

Built · Pre-launch Journal · Habit · Mood

Journal, habits and mood in one calm app — $29.99 once, offline, no account.

App Store link — added at launch

Why we’re building this

  • Journaling, habit tracking and mood logging are one daily ritual split across three apps — three subscriptions, three streak systems, three places your most private writing can leak.
  • Daily Life Suite reunites them in a single calm app in the light-blue porcelain design, and sells it the way software used to be sold: once.

The problem with current apps

  • The leading journal apps now charge a yearly subscription to hold your own diary, and lock export and sync behind it.
  • Habit apps punish a missed day by torching your streak — the fastest way to make someone quit.
  • Mood trackers reduce a day to an emoji.
  • And almost all of them require an account before you can write a word.

What it solves

  • One ritual, three parts: journal entries, habits and a simple 1–5 mood check-in (one per day) that together produce real insight — like which habits actually move your mood.
  • Forgiving habits: rest, sick and travel day-modes protect streaks instead of breaking them, because consistency over months beats perfection for a week.
  • Voice journal with free on-device transcription: speak the entry; the recording is saved first and transcribed on-device where supported, so a failed transcription never loses the entry.
  • Private by architecture: relational on-device database with full-text search, app lock via biometrics, and versioned backup you can export and re-import — validated, merged by stable ID, never overwriting what’s already there.

Monetization strategy

  • $29.99 once.
  • No free version, no subscription, no account — the price is the pitch, aimed directly at people paying a journal app every year.
  • With no server to run, every sale after store fees is margin, and the app never needs to upsell its own users to survive.

Marketing strategy

  • Position against the incumbents’ renewal emails: “Your journal shouldn’t charge rent.” Target journaling and mindfulness communities, Day One and Stoic switchers, and App Store search for pay-once alternatives.
  • The calm, light-blue design is the creative — screenshots that look like a paper journal, not a SaaS dashboard.

Fitness Suite

In design · Mockup complete Run · Gym · Sleep

Three fitness apps in one — $34.99 for life, no subscription, no account.

App Store link — added at launch

Why we’re building this

  • Training, running and sleep are one system — sleep decides what today’s workout should be, and the run plan depends on both.
  • Yet each is sold as a separate subscription.
  • Fitness Suite is a single bundle — Gym, Run and Sleep — where the three inform each other, sold once at $35 instead of rented three times forever.

The problem with current apps

  • The category leaders charge $80–$100 a year each; a lifter who also runs and tracks sleep can be $250+ a year into apps that don’t talk to each other.
  • The data is cloud-locked behind accounts, plans ignore recovery, and cancelling means losing your training history.
  • Meanwhile the proof that pay-once works is sitting in the same category: the #1 top-paid health app is a one-time purchase.

What it solves

  • One app, four surfaces designed so far: Today (one hero workout, not a dashboard), Workouts (with a live workout player — Start in two taps), Progress (volume, PRs and consistency, no leaderboards) and Plans (8-week, level-based plans, Mon–Sat with Sunday as rest/mobility). The dedicated Run and Sleep tabs are the remaining design work.
  • Connected training: last night’s sleep shapes today’s session intensity; run volume and gym volume share one weekly picture.
  • Offline and account-free: plans, logs and history live on the device. Your decade of training data is never hostage to a subscription.
  • Honest scope: no social feed, no streak-shaming — a training log that respects the person using it.

Monetization strategy

  • Paid-only at $34.99 lifetime — no free tier, no subscription, no ads.
  • That prices it at roughly five months of one competitor’s subscription, forever.
  • Realistic year one is 1,000–5,000 paid downloads ($175K gross at the top of that range), which for a solo builder with zero server costs is a business, not a side project.

Marketing strategy

  • Lead with the arithmetic: “Costs less than 5 months of the app you’re renting.” Target lifting and running communities where subscription complaints are a recurring thread, App Store search on pay-once intent, and the portfolio’s own cross-promotion — every Daily Life and InvoiceNest user is one settings-screen mention away.

Hindu Pregnancy

In design · Mockup complete Garbha Sanskar · Pregnancy

Garbha sanskar for the phone age — stories, values and ritual, week by week.

App Store link — added at launch

Why we’re building this

  • Hindu tradition has a name for what this app does — garbha sanskar, the practice of nourishing the baby’s mind and values before birth through story, music and the mother’s state of mind.
  • Families practise it today with books, grandparents and YouTube playlists.
  • This app gives it a week-by-week structure, built as its own product with its own stories and rituals.

The problem with current apps

  • Hindu mothers get the same clinical trackers as everyone else, plus a scattered aftermarket: story PDFs in family group chats, sanskar playlists on video platforms, advice of wildly varying quality.
  • Nothing brings the week’s development, the story, the music and the value together in one daily place, in order, across the whole pregnancy.

What it solves

  • The same 15-minute daily ritual: meditation, talking to the baby (Garbh Samvad), a Vedic story, and the raga of the week — one of each repeated all week so the baby hears a familiar pattern.
  • A full week view, Mon–Sun: story, meditation, raga, gentle movement, a daily nourish tip (like iron + vitamin C pairings), and the partner’s two days — Thu & Sat, Arjun reads the week’s line so both voices become familiar.
  • Gentle tracking: a daily check-in (mood, water, body, sleep), a bump diary with a weekly photo and a letter to the baby that becomes a keepsake book at the birth, and the next OB visit.
  • Honest promise: no “make your baby a genius” claims — a calm mother, a familiar voice, and bonding, in English + हिन्दी, completely free with no paywall.

Monetization strategy

  • Free, with ads and affiliate offers confined to parent areas, and a $3/month premium under evaluation as the ad-free alternative.
  • The long-term value is the family relationship — the pregnancy app hands off to Tiny Neuron after birth, where a family’s lifetime value is estimated at $20–$45 over two to three years.

Marketing strategy

  • Channels: Hindu parenting communities and creators, temple and cultural mother-and-baby groups, and the diaspora audience searching for garbha sanskar content in English.
  • The baby voice app is being explored worldwide (excluding India) once the model is proven.

Tiny Neuron

In design · Content complete — 156 weeks Child Development · 10 months – 5 years

After the birth, the plan continues — a story, activities and one value, every week of early childhood.

App Store link — added at launch

Why we’re building this

  • The pregnancy app ends at the birth — but that is exactly when parents start asking “what should I actually do with my baby today?” Tiny Neuron is the continuation: the same family, the same weekly rhythm, now for the child.
  • A week-by-week development plan from 10 months to 5 years, built from a complete curriculum written before a line of the app: 156 weeks covering 10 months to 4 years, each with a theme, a value, a story, three activities, a game and a values activity, laid out Monday to Sunday.

The problem with current apps

  • Milestone apps tell you what your baby should be doing and leave you anxious about how to help.
  • Activity content online is the opposite problem — endless unsequenced ideas, heavy on prep and shopping, with no sense of what comes this week versus in six months, and no explanation of why any of it matters.
  • Parents get either a checklist or a firehose.

What it solves

  • A plan, not a feed: every week has one theme and one value (Week 1: “Little hands, big reach” · Curiosity), a story repeated across the week, three activities with rotating types — outdoor, sensory, music, free-play, calm-routine, social — plus a game and a values activity, scheduled Mon–Sun.
  • Instructions a tired parent can follow: each activity is 3–10 minutes, uses household objects, and comes with numbered steps, a parent tip, and the exact phrases to say (“You did that!” · “Try again, you’re learning”).
  • The science, in one line: every item carries a short science note — why the pincer grasp matters, why hiding games wire the prefrontal cortex — so parents trust the plan instead of second-guessing it.
  • One continuous journey: Hindu Pregnancy hands off into Tiny Neuron at the birth, so the family’s daily ritual never breaks — it just grows up with the child.

Monetization strategy

  • Tiny Neuron inherits the family model: it arrives as the continuation for parents already using the pregnancy app, so distribution is largely built in.
  • Monetization follows the same rules as the family model — affiliate and parent-area offers only, nothing advertised inside the child-facing activities, and a simple $3/month family premium under evaluation as the ad-free option across the pregnancy-to-childhood journey.

Marketing strategy

  • The funnel is the product line itself: every Hindu Pregnancy user is offered Tiny Neuron at the birth, at the moment of highest intent.
  • Beyond that, the weekly plan is inherently shareable — one activity a day is a natural short-video format for parenting communities — and the curriculum’s specificity (“what to do with a 10-month-old this week”) is built for search in a way generic activity content is not.
